newsitem.title: USA: U.S. fixes plan to dispose of 50 tons of plutonium.
newsitem.headline: U.S. fixes plan to dispose of 50 tons of plutonium.

text.p: The Energy Department was to announce plans on Monday to dispose of 50 tons of surplus plutonium from nuclear weapons by immobilizing part in glass and burning the rest in nuclear power plants, officials said.

They said the department was taking the advice of the National Academy of Science and adopting a two-pronged program meant to reduce stocks of weapons-grade plutonium potentially available to fall into enemy hands.
Experts say it takes only a few pounds of high-grade plutonium to make a bomb capable of doing considerable damage and releasing deadly radioactive fallout.
Details were to be discussed at a news conference led by Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary, but the Washington Post obtained and published the basic information in advance.

Officials confirmed that one aspect of the disposal program envisioned a process called vitrification in which part of the surplus plutonium would be immobilized in glass or ceramic blocks and stored underground.

The rest would be combined with conventional nuclear fuel as mix-oxide, or "MOX," and used in nuclear power plants. That will cut the residue of plutonium roughly in half although it will also produce a more dangerous spent fuel than conventional nuclear-reactor waste.
Nuclear arms control advocates oppose the plan to re-use plutonium in commercial reactors, saying it will entrench the commercial production of plutonium instead of discouraging it.
This, they say, goes against the Clinton administration's policy of non-proliferation of weapons-grade plutonium and efforts to reduce the nuclear threat after the Cold War.

"Plutonium is one of the most serious security threats facing the world. What DOE (the Department of Energy) is proposing will increase nuclear dangers by entrenching pork-barrel interests in plutonium in Russia and creating them anew in the U.S.," Arjun Makhijani, president of the Institute for Energy and Environmental Research, said in a statement.
Makhijani said the U.S. plan would encourage Russia to build a MOX plant, which would perpetuate commercial production of plutonium there.
He said all of the waste should be vitrified, which is a costly and technically difficult process.
The vitrified plutonium eventually could be reclaimed, but Makhijani said it would be done under international agreement if plutonium becomes an economically-viable energy source.
The Nuclear Energy Institute, which represents the U.S. commercial nuclear power industry, favored reuse of the plutonium in commercial power plants.

"The industry believes that combining surplus plutonium with uranium to make 'mixed oxide' fuel for nuclear power plants is the best way to prevent plutonium from being reused for weapons," the NEI said in a statement. "This proven technology consumes significant amounts of plutonium and generates clean electricity."
The government would be expected to pay utilities to use the plutonium because of the problems they would encounter with community opposition and additional regulations.
